subject: Billing units: context ceiling, rounding, and minimums for clinical-summary workload

Subject: Clarifying billing for long-context clinical summarization

Hi Irene / Karthik,

Thanks again for the quick demo last week — the model latency and accuracy look promising. Before we move ahead with the pilot, our procurement and engineering teams need a clearer picture of how Redwood will bill for our workload. A couple of specifics: 

- Many clinical notes we send are multi-visit histories that push prompt windows well past 10k tokens (we have a fair number in the 12–25k range). How does Redwood treat requests that are longer than a single context window? Do you split and bill per-chunk or by a session-level aggregation?
- We also stream partial summaries back to our UI (small interim responses). If a user sends a 20k-token history but only requests a short 200-token summary on each interaction, what gets charged? Do streaming fragments trigger additional minimums?
- Finally, some of our traffic is very bursty (large nightly batches + small interactive calls). Are there rounding/minimum floors that will materially affect our pilot economics?

I've attached a small trace file (opal_billing_sample.csv) with representative request/response token counts. Can you provide a worked example invoice line or two so our finance team can map it into our budget model?

Elena

Hi Elena — thanks for the trace and clear questions. I've summarized how our billing model applies to the patterns you described and included two worked examples below. I also uploaded a short explainer (redwood_pricing_note.pdf) to the Drive link in the thread.

Summary (short answers):
- Long contexts: We bill on token consumption after model-side tokenization. For inputs longer than a single configured context window we support two behaviors depending on deployment: 1) context-splitting (per-chunk billing) for stateless calls; 2) session-aggregation for stateful sessions where KV caching is maintained — in the latter case we bill the total unique tokens processed but apply prefix reuse discounts where identical prefixes are re-used across requests.
- Streaming fragments: Each response fragment contributes to the output token tally, but we apply per-request minimums based on our meter quantum (8 tokens) and a small per-call floor (32 tokens) to avoid microbilling noise on many very small interactive calls. Streaming does not double-bill the input tokens — only the output tokens streamed plus any new input tokens not covered by cached KV state.
- Bursty vs steady: We round each billed item to the nearest quantum and apply a per-request floor as above. For pilots we typically offer a smoothing concession (monthly true-up smoothing) to help with burstiness.

Worked examples (from your CSV):
1) Nightly batch job (stateless chunking):
- Raw request: single 20,480 token patient history submitted as a single job. Model context limit: 8,192 tokens. We split into 3 chunks (8,192 + 8,192 + 4,096).
- Billing: each chunk billed on its tokenized input + output. If outputs are 600, 590, and 420 tokens respectively, billed tokens before rounding = (8,192+600) + (8,192+590) + (4,096+420) = 30,290 tokens.
- Metering quantum = 8 tokens; per-request floor = 32 tokens. After rounding to quantum and floors the total billed = 30,296 tokens (example calculation in attached PDF).

2) Interactive flow (session with KV caching):
- Initial call: send 12,300-token history -> model stores KV for the active prefix; first summary request generates 450 tokens output. Billed unique input tokens = 12,300 + 450 output = 12,750, rounded -> 12,752.
- Subsequent short request (same session): send a small 120-token addition; output 180 tokens. Because prefix was cached, only the incremental 120 input + 180 output are billed = 300 -> rounding floor to 304.
- Net effect: session-aggregation yields much lower incremental billing for short follow-ups versus re-packing the entire history each time.

Concessions we can offer for pilots:
- One-month smoothing: monthly invoice will include a smoothing adjustment that averages bursty batch usage across the month to prevent one-time spikes from blowing budget forecasts.
- Minimum-waiver: for this pilot we can waive the per-request floor for interactive calls under 1,000 tokens when traffic is clearly low-frequency (will require MAP language).

I'll copy in Karthik to discuss the MAP wording and the discount threshold. Attached links: redwood_pricing_note.pdf (walkthrough of rounding math and sample invoice rows).

Irene / Marissa — quick internal note and proposed pilot terms to present back to Opal: 

Proposed pilot concessions (for review):
1) Smoothing: apply a monthly smoothing true-up that caps any single invoice line to no more than 2x the 30-day rolling average for the pilot period (60-day lookback at the end of pilot).
2) Minimum-waiver: waive per-request floor for interactive calls under 1,000 billed tokens up to 50k waived tokens across the pilot (applies only to session-aggregated interactions, not stateless batch chunking).
3) Price hold: lock model per-token list price for pilot duration (90 days) with a 5% pilot discount on top of list for the first 3 months if Opal commits to a 6-month evaluation.

Marissa — can you confirm whether finance can approve the 50k waived tokens and 5% pilot discount under the OPAL-2025-03 deal? If not, what's the alternate threshold we should offer?

Karthik
